judged_text: Both computed schema keys, [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()], evaluate to the literal property name "[object Object]" (the second silently overwrites the first), so the "any number property is the expiry" catch-all described in the comment does not exist and z.object strips every real field except access_token. In sync mode no expiry field (expiry_date/expires_in) is ever validated or preserved: Office365 credentials keep their stale expired expiry_date and hit the parent sync endpoint on every calendar operation, and Zoom credentials lose expires_in entirely, forcing a refresh per call.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` defines computed keys as `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. Both `z.string().toString()` expressions evaluate to a literal string like `"[object Object]"`, so the second overwrites the first and there is no real “any numeric property” catch-all. Since `z.object(...)` strips unknown keys by default, in sync mode the schema effectively preserves only `access_token` (plus the bogus `"[object Object]"` key), dropping real expiry fields (`expiry_date`, `expires_in`, etc.). This matches the finding’s downstream impact: e.g., Office365 merges `tokenResponse.data` into existing credentials, but in sync mode the expiry won’t be updated; and Zoom’s refreshed token parsing in sync mode would not retain `expires_in`.
